sampling: Prose paragraphs of the body (headings, tables, fences, images excluded; 142 in total), paragraph 3 and every third after it (3, 6, ..., 141); 15 claims drawn from those paragraphs and the tables/code they introduce.

score_evidence.A: Two heading-only H2 shells, each followed directly by another H2: L299 '## 하드웨어 백엔드별 설치: CUDA, ROCm, TPU, Apple Silicon, CPU' then L302 '## 하드웨어 백엔드마다 다른 설치 경로와 따로 받는 커널'; L610 '## vLLM 선택 기준: ...' then L613 '## 동시 요청이 많을수록 커지는 vLLM의 이점과 그 한계'. Sources list duplicates entries: L661/L679 (Quickstart, '/' and '.html'), L667/L680 (the same 2023 blog post on vllm.ai and blog.vllm.ai). Front matter (two-level categories, use_math with $$ present, 131-char description), 40 paired fences and tables are otherwise fine.
score_evidence.B: Register is a consistent '입니다'. Deductions: formulaic intros repeated with the same shape: L83 '숫자로 따라가 보면 이렇습니다.', L172 '숫자를 넣어 보면 절감 규모를 가늠할 수 있습니다.', L268 '구체적인 숫자로 따라가 보면 동작이 잘 보입니다.', L133 '최악의 경우를 계산해 보면 크기를 짐작할 수 있습니다.' (rewrite: state the number directly). Noun frame L211 '이 그림에서 볼 곳은 제어가 한 점에 모인다는 부분입니다.' (rewrite: '그림에서는 제어가 한곳에 모입니다.'). Term drift between '반복' (L246-276) and 'iteration' (L490 '한 iteration에', L517 'iteration당'), 'forward마다' L527. Mechanical attribution frame repeated: L51 '서드파티인 Runpod 글은', L65 '서드파티인 Introl 블로그는', L109 '서드파티 해설(...)은', L137, L139.
score_evidence.C: Symbol collision: B is the block size at L49 ('블록 크기 $$B$$') and the per-iteration token budget at L262-265 ('토큰 상한 $$B$$', c_t = min(L_t, B - n_t)). Dangling reference L268 '토큰 상한을 앞서 든 예시값으로 두고': no example value for max_num_batched_tokens is given anywhere before (L256 gives none); the reader must infer 2,048 from the diagram. Running example referenced before it exists: L133 '이 글의 실행 예시 모델도', L193 '실행 예시의 채팅 서버에서는' precede the first naming of Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct at L172 and the first server at L344/L462 (L41 only says '모델 하나를 실행 예제로 정해'). The OS analogy is restated nearly verbatim (L49 and L103 '블록은 페이지, 토큰은 바이트, 시퀀스는 프로세스').
score_evidence.D: Hard parts get real help: the block-wise attention formula is unpacked symbol by symbol (L79) with a B=4, 10th-token walk-through (L83); copy-on-write gets a ref-count trace (L174-181); chunked prefill gets an iteration table (L270-274). Deduction: L133 announces a worst-case calculation but never produces a number (15 tokens x 800 KB = 12 MB per request vs. up to 1.4 GB contiguous would have been the point). The gpu-memory-utilization table row L499 is hard to parse ('기존 50%가 다른 vLLM 인스턴스의 몫이면 그와 무관하게 이 인스턴스의 한도는 GPU 메모리의 90%').
score_evidence.E: Good use of tables (block size trade-off L147-150, recompute vs swap L284-289, metrics L537-542, benchmark provenance L621-630) and labelled illustrative diagrams (L53-63, L174-181, L219-230). Deduction: the figure at L634 is perf_a100_n3_light.png (A100 only, three parallel outputs per request in the blog), but L632 and its alt text say '요청당 출력이 하나일 때의 결과... A100과 A10G 두 GPU 모두에서'. No visual for the request lifecycle across scheduler states beyond prose.
score_evidence.F: Checked 15 sampled claims: 14 supported (one with a stale-docs caveat), 1 wrong. Wrong: L540/L554 metric 'vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc' (and L541 'vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds_bucket'): current vLLM exports 'vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc' and 'vllm:request_time_per_output_token_seconds' / 'vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds' (vllm/v1/metrics/loggers.py L620, L941-951; docs/design/metrics.md L27); the old names come from the forum/GuideLLM sources. Outside the sample: the L632/L634 figure caption is wrong (see E). Caveat: L341 '현재 이 휠은 Python 3.12, ROCm 7.0, glibc >= 2.35' matches the quickstart note but the GPU install page (in Sources, L664) now says ROCm 10.0 is the default and rocm700 covers only 0.14.0-0.18.0. Omission rather than invention: L473 presents --api-key as protecting the server, while the docs warn it authenticates only /v1, /v2, /inference and leaves /invocations open.
score_evidence.T1: Many real commands match the docs (uv/pip install, download-kernels, attention backend, CPU image, Python-only build, docker run, serve flags, KEDA values). But the running example is never exercised end to end: no client request (curl or OpenAI client) to the 'chat server' anywhere in the post; the offline script (L426-439) never prints outputs; the config-file section (L482-486) never shows '--config' or a YAML file; the CPU source build (L353-357) omits the build-requirements install the docs require before '--no-build-isolation'; the HPA snippet (L598-608) starts at top-level 'advanced:' while the docs nest it under 'keda:'; the metrics script watches a metric name current vLLM no longer exports.
score_evidence.T2: Covers the topics in the sources in a sensible order: problem, PagedAttention, allocation, sharing/prefix caching, process architecture, scheduling/preemption, install, build, offline, serve, tuning, metrics/autoscaling, choice. Some padding from older-version pages (L240 executor backend rule, L293 preemption-mode, L527 CPU offload) labelled as v0.6.4/v0.7.3.
score_evidence.T3: Strong internals: kernel fusion and warp-per-block (L85-93), block pool/free list and slot_mapping in V1 (L135-141), prefix-cache eviction order (L201), hash-collision risk (L203), AsyncLLM/EngineCore split (L213-230), TP broadcast (L236-238), all-or-nothing preemption (L278-293), saturation metrics and KEDA fallback/scale-to-zero (L529-608), limits at batch size 1 (L640-642). Deductions: API-key auth limitations (unprotected /invocations) missing from the security discussion; several flags/defaults are given only from old docs (v0.6.4/v0.7.3 executor backend and preemption-mode, CPU offload), named as such but with no current equivalent; V1 internals rest mainly on third-party write-ups.

examples.claim: A 2,048-token OPT-13B request uses about 1.6 GB of KV cache (800 KB per token).
examples.source: arXiv 2309.06180 §3: 'the KV cache of a single token demands 800 KB ... the memory required to store the KV cache of one request can be as much as 1.6 GB.'

examples.claim: The June 2023 vLLM blog reports up to 24x higher throughput than HuggingFace Transformers without model architecture changes.
examples.source: Blog: 'it delivers up to 24x higher throughput than HuggingFace Transformers, without requiring any model architecture changes.'
Blog: 'near-optimal memory usage, with a mere waste of under 4%.'

examples.claim: Authors set the default block size to 16 (paper-era default).
examples.source: Paper §7.2: 'Accordingly, vLLM sets its default block size as 16.'

examples.claim: Sharing cuts parallel-sampling/beam-search memory by up to 55% and raises throughput up to 2.2x.
examples.source: Blog: 'cutting their memory usage by up to 55%. This can translate into up to 2.2x improvement in throughput.'

examples.claim: --prefix-caching-hash-algo selects the hash; a non-cryptographic hash raises collision risk, possibly undefined behaviour or private-data leaks in multi-tenant setups.
examples.source: vllm/config/cache.py prefix_caching_hash_algo docstring: 'Use of a hashing algorithm that is not considered cryptographically secure theoretically increases the risk of hash collisions, which can cause undefined behavior or even leak private information in multi-tenant environments.'

examples.claim: v0.6.4/v0.7.3: mp if PP x TP <= available GPUs, else ray if installed, else fail; in v0.6.4 TPU and HPU support only Ray.
examples.source: v0.6.4 engine args --distributed-executor-backend: '... “mp” will be used to keep processing on a single host. Otherwise, this will default to “ray” if Ray is installed and fail otherwise. Note that tpu and hpu only support Ray for distributed inference.'

examples.claim: Common prerequisites are Linux and Python 3.11-3.14.
examples.source: docs/getting_started/installation/gpu.md L28 and cpu.md L33: 'Python: 3.11 -- 3.14'; pyproject requires-python '>=3.11,<3.15'.

examples.claim: The ROCm wheel currently supports Python 3.12, ROCm 7.0, glibc >= 2.35.
examples.source: quickstart.md L63 note: 'It currently supports Python 3.12, ROCm 7.0 and glibc >= 2.35.' But the GPU install page (live, changed 2026-10-18 #58761): 'To install the latest version of vLLM for Python 3.12, ROCm 10.0 and glibc >= 2.35'; rocm700 covers 0.14.0-0.18.0 only.

examples.claim: Precompiled wheels appear 1-2 hours after a main commit; the installer searches up to 20 commits back and errors if csrc/ etc. changed.
examples.source: GPU install page: 'Wheels are published an hour or two after a commit lands on main ... searching up to 20 commits back. It stops with an error if compiled sources or build configuration (csrc/, cmake/, ...) changed'.

examples.claim: Current --gpu-memory-utilization is a per-instance limit; unspecified default is 1.0 with the extensible KV cache, else 0.92; v0.6.4 treated it as a global limit (0.9 with 50% used gives 40%).
examples.source: vllm/config/cache.py L216-227: 'This is a per-instance limit ... If unspecified, 1.0 with the extensible KV cache (sized from measured memory) and 0.92 otherwise'; v0.6.4: 'This is a global gpu memory utilization limit ... then only 40% of the gpu memory will be allocated'.

examples.claim: --max-model-len -1 or auto picks the largest length that fits; --kv-cache-dtype auto uses the model dtype; v0.6.4 FP8 KV without a scaling JSON defaults factors to 1.0.
examples.source: vllm/config/model.py L266 '-1 or 'auto' -> Automatically choose the maximum model length that fits in GPU memory'; cache.py L238-239 'If "auto", will use model data type'; v0.6.4 --quantization-param-path: 'Otherwise, KV cache scaling factors default to 1.0, which may cause accuracy issues.'

examples.claim: production-stack example KEDA: scale up above 5 waiting requests, poll every 15 s, 360 s cooldown; fallback after 3 failures keeps 2 replicas.
examples.source: KEDA page: 'Scale up when the queue exceeds 5 pending requests Check metrics every 15 seconds Wait 360 seconds before scaling down'; 'fallback: failureThreshold: 3 replicas: 2'.

examples.claim: LMSYS: FastChat-vLLM handled up to 5x more traffic, cut serving GPUs by 50%, 30K requests/day average and 60K peak.
examples.source: Blog: '(up to 5x more traffic) ... cut the number of GPUs used for serving the above traffic by 50%. vLLM has been handling an average of 30K requests daily and a peak of 60K'.

examples.claim: Table cells: n=1 14-24x vs HF, 2.2-2.5x vs TGI; n=3 8.5-15x vs HF, 3.3-3.5x vs TGI; LLaMA-7B on A10G, LLaMA-13B on A100.
examples.source: Blog: 'vLLM achieves 14x - 24x higher throughput than HF and 2.2x - 2.5x higher throughput than TGI' / '8.5x - 15x higher throughput than HF and 3.3x - 3.5x higher throughput than TGI'; 'LLaMA-7B on an NVIDIA A10G GPU and LLaMA-13B on an NVIDIA A100 GPU (40GB)'.

examples.claim: Server exports 'vllm:gpu_cache_usage_perc' (KV cache usage) and 'vllm:time_per_output_token_seconds_bucket'; the /metrics script watches gpu_cache_usage_perc.
examples.source: Current main vllm/v1/metrics/loggers.py L620 name='vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc'; L941/L951 'vllm:inter_token_latency_seconds', 'vllm:request_time_per_output_token_seconds'; docs/design/metrics.md L27 lists vllm:kv_cache_usage_perc. No gpu_cache_usage_perc in current source.

outside_sample.source: The embedded image is perf_a100_n3_light.png, the blog's A100 figure for three parallel output completions per request.
